subject: Public Administration
title: I. Public Administration: Concepts, Approaches, and Context

segments.text: This opening unit defines public administration and works through the classic tensions and modern approaches that shape how it is practised: the balance between democratic accountability and bureaucratic expertise, the boundary between politics and administration, the trade-off between efficiency and equity, and the succession of major administrative approaches from traditional bureaucracy through New Public Management to today’s governance and New Public Service perspectives.

encompasses the institutions, personnel, and processes through which public policies and laws are implemented and public services are delivered. Its scope is genuinely broad, spanning organization design, personnel management, budgeting, policy implementation, regulation, direct service delivery, and accountability — in effect, everything between a law being passed and a citizen actually receiving the service or being subject to the regulation that law intended. It is useful to think of public administration as both an

of government, and most exam answers benefit from addressing both senses explicitly.
supplies political legitimacy: it rests on public consent, representation, and political accountability, with elected officials answerable to citizens through elections.

, in contrast, supplies continuity, technical expertise, hierarchy, and rule-based, impersonal administration — a permanent professional civil service that continues functioning across changes of elected government. The productive resolution of this tension, not a choice of one over the other, is the exam-relevant point: elected leaders set lawful policy direction, while professional administrators implement it impartially and provide candid, technically-informed advice regardless of which party holds office. The same bureaucratic features that create predictability and continuity (rules, hierarchy, written records) can also produce
when rules become ends in themselves rather than means to public purposes — a risk worth naming explicitly whenever bureaucracy’s strengths are discussed.

(associated with Woodrow Wilson and Frank Goodnow) separated the political choice of goals (properly the domain of elected officials) from the administrative execution of those goals (properly the domain of professional, non-partisan administrators). In practice this boundary is not absolute, and the syllabus explicitly asks students to explain why: implementation requires interpretation of ambiguous statutory language, and administrators regularly advise political leadership on feasibility, cost, and likely consequences before a policy decision is even finalized — meaning administrators inevitably shape policy substance even while formally only “executing” it. The workable modern principle is not “no politics in administration at all,” but rather
lawful political control combined with professional, impartial administration
— political leaders set direction and exercise oversight, while administrators implement lawfully and advise honestly.

asks how much public value is produced from the resources committed — the same efficiency concept introduced in the Management unit’s discussion of Business Administration, now applied to public resources.

asks whether the resulting benefits, burdens, opportunities, and treatment are distributed fairly across citizens. These two criteria can genuinely conflict: a policy that is cheapest per unit of output (highly efficient) might systematically underserve a remote or disadvantaged population that is more expensive to reach — the classic example being rural healthcare or education delivery, where the efficient (low-cost) option is often concentrated service in accessible urban centres, at the direct expense of equitable access for rural citizens. Public management is therefore frequently a genuine balancing exercise between these two values rather than a simple maximization of either one alone.
Beyond efficiency and equity, public administration scholarship recognizes a broader constellation of values that legitimate public action:
(answerability for the use of public authority and resources),
(adherence to constitutional and statutory authority), and
(orientation toward the common good rather than narrow or private benefit). Different administrative eras and approaches, discussed next, have emphasized different subsets of these values.

The traditional model emphasizes hierarchy, formal rules, merit-based bureaucratic staffing, functional specialization, and clear lines of authority — essentially the application of Weberian bureaucratic principles (developed further in Unit II) to the machinery of the state. Its strengths are continuity, procedural consistency, and predictability; its characteristic risk, as already noted under Democracy versus Bureaucracy above, is rigidity and slow adaptation when circumstances change faster than formal rules and procedures can be revised.

emerged from the 1980s onward as a reaction against the perceived rigidities of traditional bureaucracy, introducing private-sector-style management practices into government: stronger attention to measurable results and performance indicators, greater managerial discretion (loosening rigid rule-based control in exchange for accountability for outcomes), competition and contracting-out of service delivery, and market-style mechanisms generally. The central debate the syllabus asks students to prepare is genuinely two-sided: NPM’s advocates argue it improves efficiency and responsiveness by importing disciplined management practice; its critics argue that treating citizens as “customers” and importing market logic can fragment coordinated public action, weaken democratic accountability (since contracted-out services are harder for citizens to hold directly accountable), and crowd out non-market public values like equity and universal service.

, developed partly as a corrective response to NPM’s market-oriented emphasis, argues that public officials should help citizens articulate and pursue shared interests, rather than either steering markets (the traditional model’s rule-bound instinct) or treating citizens merely as individual customers (NPM’s market-oriented instinct). It emphasizes citizenship, democratic dialogue, collaborative problem-solving, and a plurality of public values beyond simple efficiency — positioning itself explicitly as a corrective to both Traditional Public Administration and NPM, a genealogy worth stating clearly in any comparative answer.

recognizes that public outcomes today are rarely produced by a single government department acting alone; they emerge from networks involving private firms, civil society organizations, communities, and multiple levels of government working together (or in tension). A precise distinction worth stating explicitly:
refers to the formal institutions of the state, while

refers to the broader process and set of relationships through which collective action and public outcomes are actually produced — governance is a wider concept than government, not a synonym for it. The practical trade-off is that networks can mobilize diverse expertise and resources beyond what any single government department could command, but they also make responsibility harder to trace when something goes wrong, making coordination and accountability mechanisms across the network especially important.

blocks.text: .12 Historical Roots of Public Administration in Pakistan

segments.text: Pakistan’s administrative structure inherited a strong

: centralized authority, a district-based field administration system, an emphasis on revenue collection and the maintenance of law and order, and an elite professional civil service modelled on the Indian Civil Service. Post-independence, these inherited institutions and structures largely persisted, but now operating within a new constitutional order, a different political context, and — critically — a developmental mandate (nation-building, economic development) that the colonial administrative apparatus was never originally designed to pursue. Much of the subsequent history of Pakistani public administration, developed further in Unit X (Governance and Administrative Reforms), can be read as a long, still-incomplete process of adapting an inherited colonial administrative machine to these newer democratic and developmental demands.

items.text: The core tensions of this unit — democracy vs. bureaucracy, politics vs. administration, efficiency vs. equity — are not meant to be resolved by choosing one side; the exam rewards explaining how each pair is balanced in practice.

The historical sequence Traditional Public Administration → New Public Management → New Public Service/Governance is a genealogy of correctives: each later approach responds to specific limitations of the one before it.

Government (formal state institutions) and governance (the broader network of actors producing public outcomes) are distinct concepts, frequently confused, and worth stating precisely whenever either term appears in an answer.
